title: AI document processing: which AI reads files with no wrong numbers
description: We benchmarked AI tools on 30 sealed fund reports. Which ones made no mistakes, what each costs per page, and three ways to build it.
summary: AI document processing turns PDFs, scans and forms into fields your systems can use. Reading the text is now cheap: basic OCR is $1.50 per 1,000 pages at AWS, Google and Azure[^2][^3][^4]. The hard part is knowing which fields came out wrong, on your files rather than a vendor's demo set[^20]. We built a benchmark to find out[^7].
verdict: Have a frontier model read the raw PDF, have a second model read it too, and send only the facts they disagree on to a person. Research finds that checking answers against a second model or a second run catches errors[^15][^16]. In our sealed benchmark of 30 fund reports, the two best models made zero mistakes at $0.12 to $0.15 per report[^7]. Don't trust a model's own confidence score: wrong answers came back rated 70 to 100[^7], and published studies find models overconfident[^14].

pickElse: You process thousands of standard invoices or receipts a day: a cloud prebuilt parser costs about $10 per 1,000 pages at AWS, Azure and Google[^2][^4][^3] and handles volume for you.

Your files cannot leave your network: run open-source Docling (MIT licence)[^6] or a local model. Expect more wrong values: in our first round the two local models made 8 wrong values each where Claude Haiku 5.5 made none[^7].
You only need searchable text, not fields: basic OCR is about $1.50 per 1,000 pages at all three big clouds[^2][^3][^4].

ownData.title: Our benchmark: 30 fund reports, keys sealed before any AI read them
ownData.intro: FinExtractBench is Zavient's own benchmark. We picked 30 public private-fund reports (781 pages), wrote the correct answer for every fact by hand and locked the answers before any tool ran[^7]. A mistake is a wrong value, a value the report never states, or an event it does not support. Each tool read each raw PDF once.
ownData.note: Limits: one person wrote the answers; the reports are digital, in English and at most 56 pages[^7]. Zero mistakes in 30 reports still allows a true rate of up to about 1 report in 10[^19]. A scan check on 10 of the reports, as page pictures, also found 0 mistakes for both tools[^7]. When the two tools disagreed, 66 facts went to a person, about 2 per report[^7].

example.input: A 57-page quarterly report from a private equity fund, as a PDF.
example.output: Committed capital, paid-in capital, distributions, net asset value, DPI and TVPI, each with the page number and the exact words it came from, plus a flag on any fact the two models disagree on.

tables.title: Hard round: every answer had to quote its page
tables.intro: Eight public fund reports, two of them 47 and 57 pages long. A fact counts only if it is right and the quoted words are on the cited page. One run each, on cleaned text[^7].
tables.note: Source: FinExtractBench, Zavient, 21 Nov 2026[^7]. The top nine tools were within 2 facts of each other, so pick on wrong answers, cost and speed. All 8 reports have since been read while fixing the answers, so they are no longer unseen[^7].

howToTest: Pick 50 real files, including your worst scans and longest reports. Include facts some files do not state, to catch invented answers. Even vendors advise benchmarking on your own documents[^20].
Write the right answer for every fact before any AI reads the files, and lock it, so the AI's output cannot sway it.
Require each answer to name its page and quote the exact words, and have code check that the quote is there.
Count wrong answers apart from blanks. A blank goes to a person; a wrong number can slip through.
Compare cost and time per file, and run the winner again on new files before you go live.

buyVsBuild.buy: Buy a prebuilt parser or an AP tool when your files are standard invoices, receipts or IDs, which the clouds' prebuilt models already cover[^2][^4], and you mainly need volume and an audit trail.
buyVsBuild.build: Build on frontier models when your files are specific to your business, the facts feed your own systems, and a wrong number is expensive. The build is small: a prompt, a fact list, a checker and a review queue where your team decides the hard cases. In our benchmark that queue got about 2 facts per report[^7].

watchOuts: Vendor accuracy numbers mostly come from the vendor's own benchmark runs[^20]. Even on our sealed set, the AI was right and our hand-written answer was wrong in 22 of 57 disputes[^7]. Public benchmark answer keys have errors too[^18]. Check your answer key.
A model that writes a plausible wrong number is worse than one that leaves the field blank[^17]. Score them separately.
Two tables on one page with similar labels fooled 7 of 10 tools in our hard round[^7]. Check the facts that sit near look-alikes.

Prices and model versions change. Mistral, for one, lists OCR 3 at $2 and OCR 4.1 at $4 per 1,000 pages[^8]. Re-run your benchmark when either changes, and keep the files and answers so the re-run is cheap.
Read the vendor's data terms. Datalab's rate card shows prices with a 25% discount that assumes you let it train on your data[^12].

sources.name: Xiong et al., Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty? (2023)
sources.what: Finds that language models tend to be overconfident when they state their own confidence.

sources.name: Cohen et al., LM vs LM (EMNLP 2023)
sources.what: Having a second model question the first catches factual errors better than earlier methods, often by a large gap.

sources.name: Manakul et al., SelfCheckGPT (EMNLP 2023)
sources.what: Facts that disagree across several answers to the same question are likely invented; consistent facts are likely true.

sources.name: OpenAI, Why language models hallucinate (2025)
sources.what: Argues errors are worse than abstentions and evaluations should penalise confident errors more than uncertainty.

sources.name: Northcutt et al., Pervasive label errors in test sets (2021)
sources.what: Finds at least 3.3% wrong answers on average across 10 widely used benchmark answer keys.

sources.name: Newman, JAMA 1995, interpreting small numerators
sources.what: With zero events in N trials, the upper 95% confidence limit for the true rate is about 3/N.

rules.name: EU AI Act, Annex III
rules.what: Reading documents is not a high-risk use on its own. It becomes part of one when the facts feed credit scoring of people or life and health insurance pricing[^21]. Then logging and human oversight apply[^22][^23]. These rules start on 2 December 2027[^24][^25].

rules.name: Regulation B, 12 CFR 1002.9
rules.what: If extracted facts feed a US credit decision, a decline still needs specific reasons[^26], even when an algorithm made it[^27]. A wrongly read fact becomes a wrong reason, so keep the page and quote behind every fact.

rules.name: NYDFS Circular Letter No. 7
rules.what: New York insurers that use AI in underwriting and pricing stay responsible for vendor tools[^28]. Where available, their vendor contracts should give them audit rights[^28].
